failing_part: t reference on the number of participants minus 2 degrees of freedom, since each participant contributes one residual to the sandwich variance
narrowest_regime: Nowhere in a cluster-randomized trial: the sandwich variance sums cluster-level score contributions, so the reference df is set by the number of clusters (K minus 2 for intercept and arm). Participant-level df approaches the normal and is only harmless with many clusters (roughly K of 40 or more).
reason: The robust (sandwich) variance is built from one score vector per cluster, not per participant, so the effective sample for the variance is K clusters; Li & Redden recommend a t reference with K-2 df (with a bias-corrected sandwich) and say the Wald z-test should be avoided with few clusters. Simulation (Gaussian outcome, 50 per cluster, ICC 0.05, exchangeable GEE, robust SE, K=10): nominal-5% test rejects 11.8% with t(N-2 = 498 df) versus 7.4% with t(K-2 = 8 df); at K=20 it is 5.8% versus 4.8%. The participant-df rule is the anti-conservative choice, though the uncorrected sandwich is still liberal at K=10.

citations.cite: Li P, Redden DT. Small sample performance of bias-corrected sandwich estimators for cluster-randomized trials with binary outcomes. Stat Med 2015;34:281-296 (abstract fetched: z-test to be avoided with few clusters, t approximation with KC/FG correction; the K-2 df detail is from the paper body, not fetched)

bite_note: With under 40 clusters the interval half-width and p-value change materially (t critical value 2.3 at 8 df vs 1.96); participant-level df gives intervals that are too narrow and a Type I error of about 12% at K=10.

failing_part: A feature whose D-ratio ... is 50% or less ... is removed
narrowest_regime: The correct rule is the reverse: remove features whose D-ratio (QC SD over sample SD) exceeds 50%; keep those at or below it. The remaining details (QC SD frozen before the seal, study SD from training folds) are engineering choices not checked here.
reason: Broadhurst et al. define D-ratio = SD_QC / SD_sample x 100% and recommend an acceptance criterion of at most below 50% (preferably much lower), removing metabolites above it; a D-ratio near 100% means no biological variance, and the closer to zero the better. As written the claim removes the best-measured features (low technical-to-total SD) and keeps the noisiest, and its own stated rationale (too little biological variance relative to technical) describes a HIGH D-ratio. At D = 50% technical variance is only 25% of the total, so a low ratio cannot mean 'too little biological variance'.

citations.cite: Broadhurst D et al. Guidelines and considerations for the use of system suitability and quality control samples in mass spectrometry assays applied in untargeted clinical metabolomic studies. Metabolomics 2018;14:72 (PMC5960010: D-ratio definition and <50% acceptance, higher removed)

bite_note: If implemented as written the filter would discard the most reproducible features and retain the noisiest, changing the feature set that enters every downstream model.

failing_part: a yes/no outcome with no numeric column that reads as a follow-up time is a status at sampling and is correctly analyzed as counted over one period for everyone
narrowest_regime: Cross-sectional prevalence, case-control sampling, or a cohort outcome over a fixed common window; not incident events in a cohort with variable follow-up or censoring.
reason: The absence of a recognized follow-up column does not show the outcome is a status at sampling: metabolomics, genomics and survey data are routinely cohort-derived incident events (e.g., incident disease in a prospective cohort, nested case-control), where unequal follow-up makes a plain binary model's risks and odds ratios depend on the follow-up distribution. Not asking is a reasonable default for the common cross-sectional case, but 'correctly analyzed' is stated as fact when it is an unverified assumption. No basis was offered.
bite_note: Asking would catch an unrecognized or differently named follow-up column or variable follow-up and move the analysis to time-to-event or a flagged limitation; skipping it silently fixes a binary model. The effect is modest because with no follow-up column a time-to-event model is unavailable anyway.

failing_part: the K(K-1)/2 pairwise intervals are descriptive, uncorrected for multiplicity, because the choice is corrected by BBC-CV
narrowest_regime: The corrected resampled t on rK-1 df is approximately valid (slightly conservative) as a test of one pre-specified pair's difference in expected score at training size n1. The pairwise intervals are valid per pair, but not as a family and not for a pair picked after looking at the same scores.
reason: The t statistic, the (1/(rK) + n2/n1) variance factor (n2/n1 = 1/(K-1)) and rK-1 df match Nadeau & Bengio and Bouckaert & Frank's use. Simulation with 10 x 5 repeated CV and two exchangeable OLS learners (null): corrected test rejected 3-4% at n = 50, 100 and 200 and 4% with 10 folds, versus 55-59% for the uncorrected paired t, so the correction is essential and approximately valid (conservative) there. The justification for leaving pairwise statements unadjusted does not follow: BBC-CV (Tsamardinos et al.) removes the optimistic bias in the selected configuration's estimated score; it does not control the false-'X is ahead' rate across K(K-1)/2 pairs or make an interval for a data-selected pair valid. Calling them 'descriptive' limits the damage but the 'because' is a non sequitur.

citations.cite: Nadeau C, Bengio Y. Inference for the generalization error. Mach Learn 2003;52:239-281
Bouckaert RR, Frank E. Evaluating the replicability of significance tests for comparing learning algorithms. PAKDD 2004
Tsamardinos I et al. Bootstrapping the out-of-sample predictions for efficient and accurate cross-validation (BBC-CV). Mach Learn 2018

bite_note: The correction changes 'X is ahead' sentences from false positives about half the time to roughly nominal; the unadjusted multiplicity across many pairs would still produce spurious 'ahead' statements when many families are compared.

failing_part: the sound missing-data handling for inference is multiple imputation with the group in the imputation model
narrowest_regime: Missingness at random given the observed group and other analysis variables, with MI whose imputation model also contains the outcome, the exposure and any interactions in the analysis model (including group-by-exposure terms).
reason: MI with group in the model is a valid way to handle group-dependent missingness under MAR, and complete-case analysis does need its assumption stated. But 'the sound' handling overstates: group is necessary, not sufficient (omitting the outcome or analysis-model interactions biases MI estimates toward the null), complete-case regression is also unbiased when missingness depends only on covariates included in the model (it only loses efficiency), and MI does not rescue missing-not-at-random within group. Alternatives (FIML, IPW) are also sound.

citations.cite: Sterne JAC et al. Multiple imputation for missing data in epidemiological and clinical research. BMJ 2009;338:b2393

bite_note: Sets the Recommended option on the missing-values question; a researcher whose imputation model lacks the outcome or the group interactions gets a biased estimate, whereas complete-case with group in the model could have been fine.

failing_part: below 0.003697, removing the screen moves the exposure's estimate by less than 0.1 of its 95% interval half-width
narrowest_regime: Datasets of about the size and structure of the NHANES fixture the threshold was fitted on; the share-times-SMD score is not scale-free in half-width units.
reason: The score share x largest SMD does not scale with the interval half-width. A shift from dropping rows is roughly (share x covariate shift x effect heterogeneity), which does not fall with n, while the half-width falls as 1/sqrt(n), so the shift in half-width units grows as sqrt(n) at a fixed score (e.g., with heterogeneity 0.3 and unit error the same score of 0.0037 crosses 0.1 half-width near n of about 30,000). The cut was calibrated on 9 cases from one fixture with a simplified pipeline and one held band-0 check, so four significant digits and a guarantee about half-widths are invented precision. The direction (smaller score, smaller consequence) is plausible and the 'could bias' wording is cautious.
bite_note: Decides whether the implausible-reporter screen is reported as inconsequential (supplement line) versus a limitation sentence or action; at large n a 'doesn't change your numbers' verdict can be wrong in half-width terms.

failing_part: the UL applies to total intake; ... a share at risk of excess only if the recalls include supplements
narrowest_regime: Nutrients whose UL is defined on total intake from food, fortified food, water and supplements (e.g., vitamin D, calcium, zinc, iron, vitamin C). Not magnesium, niacin, folate, vitamin E or preformed vitamin A, where the UL applies to the supplemental or synthetic form only.
reason: For several nutrients the IOM UL excludes food (magnesium: pharmacologic/supplement magnesium only; niacin and folate: synthetic forms; vitamin E: supplemental alpha-tocopherol), so comparing total usual intake with that UL would overstate the share at risk. And 'only if supplements are included' is too strong: food-only intake above the UL already implies total intake above it, so that share is still at risk, just a lower bound. The rule is a good default label for most nutrients but not a universal.

citations.cite: Institute of Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes: Applications in Dietary Assessment (2000) and DRI UL tables (nutrient-specific UL source definitions); NIH ODS fact sheets (fetch blocked, recalled)

bite_note: Changes the label and interpretation of the share above a UL: 'at risk of excess' versus 'above the UL from foods alone (a lower bound)' versus, for supplement-only ULs, comparing the right intake component.

narrowest_regime: The bound is conditional, as the claim says, on exchangeability of the noise variables and on the base procedure being no worse than random guessing; correlated designs make it a heuristic, though it held in the correlated cases I ran.
reason: With q = floor(sqrt((2*tau-1)p)), q^2 <= (2*tau-1)p, so the Meinshausen-Buhlmann expression q^2/((2*tau-1)p) is at most 1. Shah & Samworth prove the same bound for complementary pairs (their abstract: no exchangeability or quality assumptions for the bound on low-selection-probability variables; the finite-B version follows from Markov on the pair-selection proportion since a selection frequency >= tau forces both-halves frequency >= 2*tau-1). Simulation (p=100, q=4, tau=0.6, B=50 pairs, 5 signals, 60 datasets): mean false selections 0.00 independent, 0.05 AR(0.8), 0.23 AR(0.95), 0.07 equicorrelated 0.5, 0.07 at n=60 with weak signal; the max never exceeded 2. The bound is very conservative, trading power for error control.

citations.cite: Meinshausen N, Buhlmann P. Stability selection. JRSS B 2010;72:417-473
Shah RD, Samworth RJ. Variable selection with error control: another look at stability selection. JRSS B 2013;75:55-80 (arXiv 1105.5578 abstract)

bite_note: The constants fix how many variables can ever be selected (q is only 4 at p=100 and 1 at p=10), which determines the selected model and the power.

narrowest_regime: Holds for batch as a fixed-effect nominal label; with two batches any coding is equivalent, and a genuinely numeric run-order or drift covariate is a different adjustment that the confirmation step is meant to distinguish.
reason: Batch identifiers are nominal, so a numeric code entered as one column imposes a linear trend across arbitrary batch labels and cannot remove step differences between batches; the standard covariate adjustment (e.g., limma removeBatchEffect, ComBat fixed form) uses one indicator per batch. Requiring the user to confirm that an integer column is a code, not a quantity, is a sound guard.
bite_note: A numeric batch column entered as-is would adjust for a linear trend in batch number instead of batch offsets, leaving the batch effect in the data.

narrowest_regime: Applies to quintiles of the exposure of interest. For a confounder, categorization leaves residual confounding that biases the exposure estimate, so 'not a false number' would not hold there (the cited decision also covers confounders).
reason: Quintile indicators give a well-defined contrast between group means (adjusted for the other covariates), losing within-quintile variation and implying a step-function dose-response, with loss of power; that is a coarser estimand, not a wrong number. Ranking below the spline (and line) on efficiency and fidelity grounds, but allowing it because it is the field's common reporting convention, is a defensible policy. Turner et al. document prevalence of the practice, not its validity.

citations.cite: Turner EL, Dobson JE, Pocock SJ. Categorisation of continuous risk factors in epidemiological publications: a survey of current practice. Epidemiol Perspect Innov 2010;7:9
Royston P, Altman DG, Sauerbrei W. Dichotomizing continuous predictors in multiple regression: a bad idea. Stat Med 2006;25:127-141

bite_note: Determines the ordering of functional-form options for the exposure and that quintiles are allowed, not blocked.

narrowest_regime: Uniform shrinkage addresses average overfitting (calibration slope) only; the bootstrap slope is the better estimator, and the out-of-fold slope fallback is noisier and biased toward over-shrinking, especially at low events per variable.
reason: Uniform shrinkage by the calibration slope with the intercept re-estimated using the shrunk linear predictor as an offset is the standard Van Houwelingen-le Cessie / Steyerberg update. Simulation (logistic, 10 predictors, n=150, about 5 events per variable, test set 40,000): raw calibration slope 0.62 and log loss 0.5053; bootstrap-shrunk 0.98 and 0.4889; CV-shrunk log loss 0.4937. But the pooled 5-fold slope averaged 0.47 against an oracle of 0.58 for the fitted models (bootstrap 0.67), with occasional near-zero or wild estimates, so the fallback over-shrinks and is variable.

citations.cite: Van Houwelingen JC, le Cessie S. Predictive value of statistical models. Stat Med 1990;9:1303-1325
Steyerberg EW. Clinical Prediction Models, 2nd ed, 2019, ch. 13
Collins GS et al. Evaluation of clinical prediction models (part 1). BMJ 2024;384:e074819

bite_note: Changes the deployed coefficients and predicted risks (shrinks them toward the mean), which improves calibration and log loss out of sample.

failing_part: models that keep total energy predict alike
narrowest_regime: Unpenalized linear and generalized linear models that contain total energy: the standard, residual and energy-partition models span the same column space and give identical predictions (Willett, Howe & Kushi 1997). Approximately so for ridge and lasso; not for tree-based models or nutrient-density (ratio) features.
reason: The equivalence is a linear-reparametrization argument, so it does not extend to nonlinear learners or to density features. Simulation (20 nutrients proportional to energy, outcome depending on nutrient density, n=400, 5 datasets): test R2 for OLS was 0.462 for the standard, residual and partition models, and 0.46 for ridge and lasso; for random forest it was 0.283 (standard, partition) versus 0.403 (residual) and 0.420 (density plus energy). So the energy parameterization changes predictions for tree models, and the choice is not purely an estimation question when the model family is nonlinear.

citations.cite: Willett WC, Howe GR, Kushi LH. Adjustment for total energy intake in epidemiologic studies. Am J Clin Nutr 1997;65(4 Suppl):1220S-1228S
Shmueli G. To explain or to predict? Stat Sci 2010;25:289-310

bite_note: For tree-ensemble or other nonlinear prediction models, not offering the choice of energy-adjusted or density features can leave measurable accuracy on the table (R2 0.28 vs 0.40 in the simulated case); for linear models it changes nothing.
